title: Are American Schools Resegregating?
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman takes on the claim, made in a This American Life interview with Nikole Hannah-Jones, that public schools are as unequal and segregated as they were 60 years ago. He notes that sixty years ago was 1966, before the Fair Housing Act and when legal segregation was only beginning to be dismantled, so the claim that so little has changed does not hold up. On the narrower resegregation story, he explains that the popular exposure index moves with changing demographics, while Steven Rivkin's dissimilarity index shows schools closer to integration than ever. Stanford's normalized exposure measure shows White-Black segregation roughly flat since 2000 and White-Hispanic segregation down about 10 percent, with exceptions inside many large districts. He then separates integration from school quality, citing Tomás Monarrez and Rucker Johnson on cross-district policies and the benefits of desegregation paired with resources. His conclusion is that children cannot wait for integration and need rigorous coursework, capable teachers and attentive adults now.
points: Aldeman argues that the claim "so little has changed" ignores the legal and demographic shifts since 1966, including the Civil Rights Act, Fair Housing Act and mass desegregation.
The resegregation narrative leans on an exposure index that moves with the falling White share of students, while the dissimilarity index shows steady improvement at the school level.
Stanford's normalized exposure data show White-Black segregation flat from 2000 to 2020 and White-Hispanic segregation down about 10 percent, though many large districts have seen increases.
Monarrez's finding that attendance zones make schools slightly more integrated than residence alone implies that cross-district policies are the main integration levers.
Integration and school quality are different goals, and Aldeman concludes that students need strong coursework, capable teachers and attentive adults regardless of who their classmates are.
quotes: Public schools are [as] unequal and segregated as they were 10 years ago, 30 years ago, 60 years ago. Um, sixty years ago was 1966.
It’s hard to square that history with the idea that “so little has changed.” Schools are significantly more equitable and less segregated than they were 60 years ago.
That narrative is misleading, in part because it relies on a measure of integration that doesn't account for America's changing demographics.
Because society as a whole has become more diverse over time and the share of students who are White has fallen, the exposure index has moved along with policy efforts.
White-Black segregation increased about 4% from 1991 to 2000 and was essentially flat from 2000 to 2020. White-Hispanic segregation actually declined by about 10% over the full period.

There are important exceptions to the national trends. The Stanford team also found that segregation has increased within many large school districts, particularly as earlier desegregation policies were abandoned.
However, integration and school quality are two different goals, and that distinction matters for understanding Hannah-Jones's experience.

But children can’t wait for their schools to become more integrated before they get a good education. They need challenging coursework, capable teachers, and adults who notice when they’re falling behind
